blurb: A cinderblock radio station on the hill under the town water tower, all blinking consoles and a call-in line that rings a little too late at night. Climb the tower ladder and you can see the whole valley.
art: A small cinderblock radio station on a grassy hilltop beneath a tall round water tower painted Glimmer Falls, a red-blinking transmitter antenna, a pickup truck parked outside, golden afternoon light over the valley

beats.title: Line Three
beats.place: The broadcast booth, KGLM 103.3
beats.text: Mix Bell lets you sit in on the afternoon show, and line three lights up. The caller asks for a song from 1958 in a voice full of bubbles, like she's calling from under water. The light on the console says the call is coming from the old quarry pay phone, which was flooded and removed in 1959.
beats.art: A teenage DJ with big headphones in a small radio booth beside a teenager, a console with a single blinking call-line button, a dusty 1958 record held up from a crate, rain on the window

choices.label: Find the record and play her song

success.text: You find the single in the station's dusty archive and Mix spins it on air. The caller sighs, happy, and the line clicks off. For the rest of the afternoon, every radio on Crystal Street plays a little warmer. Mix gives you the record.
success.art: A teenager handing a vintage vinyl single to a DJ in a radio booth, the record spinning on a turntable, a call button going dark

failure.text: You can't find the record. Mix plays something close and the caller goes very quiet, then says "That's not it" in a voice right next to your ear instead of in the headphones. The whole console fizzes.
failure.art: A radio console sparking with static in a dim booth, two teens leaning away from a microphone, a blinking call line

choices.label: Keep her talking on air

success.text: You ask her name, Lillian, and her favorite dance, the stroll. She tells you about the lake before it drained, the dock, the boy she was meeting. The town hears her on air. A dozen old folks call in to say they remember her. The line clicks off kindly.
success.art: A teenager speaking gently into a radio microphone, a phone board lighting up with incoming calls, an old photo of a lakeside dock taped to the wall

failure.text: You ask the wrong question. "Where are you?" The bubbles get louder, the line fills with rushing water, and the booth's floor is suddenly wet. Mix pulls the plug. The puddle doesn't dry for a day.
failure.art: A radio booth floor with a spreading puddle of dark water around the chair legs, a DJ yanking a cord from the console

beats.title: Halfway Up the Tower
beats.place: The water tower ladder, above KGLM
beats.text: A kid named Jun climbed the water tower to paint his crush's initials on the tank, and now he's stuck forty feet up, clinging to a ladder rung that's peeling away from the rivets. Below him is a can of red spray paint, dented. Above him, painted by someone else, letters older than both of you: GO BACK.
beats.art: A boy clinging to a rusty water tower ladder high above a hilltop, a rung pulling loose from its rivets, faded painted letters on the tank above him, a teenager looking up from the base

choices.label: Climb up and guide his feet down

success.text: You climb, steady and slow, and talk about anything else: cartoons, cereal, his crush. You guide his sneakers rung by rung. At the bottom, he tells you the crush is a boy named Theo, and he's going to tell him with words instead of paint.
success.art: A teenager on a water tower ladder guiding a younger boy's sneaker onto a rung below, sunset behind them, the valley spread out far below

failure.text: The rung snaps under your hand and for one long second you're both hanging. Mix comes running with a rope from the station and gets you both down. Jun is okay. Your hands shake until dinner.
failure.art: A snapped ladder rung falling through the air beside a water tower, two figures clinging to the ladder, a DJ running with a coil of rope

choices.label: Run inside and get on air for help

success.text: You grab the mic and ask anyone with a ladder truck to come to the KGLM hill. Within ten minutes three pickups and the volunteer fire department show up. Jun comes down in a bucket. The whole valley heard you save him.
success.art: A fire department ladder truck extended to a water tower, a boy climbing into its bucket, pickup trucks and onlookers gathered on the hill

failure.text: Your voice goes out on dead air, the transmitter hiccuping static, and nobody hears. By the time you run back out, Jun has climbed down himself, pale and furious, and the words on the tank above now read GO BACK NOW.
failure.art: A pale boy standing at the base of a water tower glaring at a teenager, painted letters high on the tank reading go back now

beats.title: Be Caller Thirteen
beats.place: A pay phone outside the Kwik Mart, then KGLM
beats.text: KGLM is giving away two tickets to the Halloween night Thrash Bash at the fairgrounds to caller number thirteen. Every phone in town is ringing the station. You've got one quarter, a pay phone and a busy signal. The busy signal, if you listen closely, is counting.
beats.art: A teenager at a strip-mall pay phone with the receiver to one ear and a quarter in hand, a convenience store glowing behind them, a radio playing on a nearby car dashboard

choices.label: Redial with lightning fingers

success.text: Eleven. Twelve. You hit the hook, redial, and Mix's voice says "Caller thirteen, you're on KGLM!" You win the tickets, which you sell to Wade for three quarters and a ride wherever you want this week.
success.art: A teenager shouting with joy into a pay phone receiver, fist in the air, a convenience store parking lot at dusk

failure.text: You get through, but you're caller fourteen. Mix sounds sorry. Then, behind him, a different voice on the line says "I'll take thirteen" and the call drops. On air, the winner never gives a name.
failure.art: A pay phone receiver dangling on its cord at a lonely strip-mall wall, a teenager staring at it

choices.label: Skip the phone and bike to the station

success.text: You pedal up the KGLM hill like your life depends on it and barge through the door just as the twelfth caller hangs up. Mix laughs so hard he lets you win in person. Also, he gives you a station mixtape for pure nerve.
success.art: A sweaty teenager bursting through a radio station door with a bike behind them, a DJ in the booth doubling over laughing

failure.text: The hill is steeper than you remember. You arrive gasping as the winner is announced, then coast all the way back down with no brakes and land in a hedge. The radio in the hedge-owner's kitchen is playing your heavy breathing on air.
failure.art: A teenager tangled in a hedge beside a crashed bicycle, a kitchen window above with a radio on the sill

beats.title: Live From Sal's Mattress Kingdom
beats.place: The production booth, KGLM 103.3
beats.text: The station manager's voice talent quit, and Sal's Mattress Kingdom's Halloween Spooktacular ad runs live in ninety seconds. The copy is three pages of puns. The manager shoves it at you. The microphone has a little piece of tape on it that says DON'T SAY IT THREE TIMES, and nobody will tell you what IT is.
beats.art: A cluttered radio production booth with a vintage microphone wrapped in a strip of tape, a panicked station manager handing a teenager pages of ad copy, an on-air light about to go red

choices.label: Read the copy like your life depends on it

success.text: "At Sal's, our prices are SO LOW, they're SIX FEET UNDER!" You nail every pun. Sal himself calls the station crying with joy. You get four quarters and a lifetime offer of a free mattress, which you decline, because nobody should own a free mattress from Sal.
success.art: A teenager leaning into a microphone with dramatic gestures in a radio booth, a station manager giving a thumbs-up through the glass

failure.text: You say "Spooktacular" three times without thinking. The on-air light flickers, the tape on the mic peels off by itself and the ad finishes in a voice that is not yours. Sal loves it. You don't sleep well.
failure.art: A strip of tape peeling off a microphone by itself in a dim radio booth, an on-air light flickering red

choices.label: Rewrite it fast into something less cursed

success.text: You cut every Spooktacular and write a jingle on the spot. Sal's sales double. The station manager pins your copy on the wall and asks if you want a job writing ads. The tape on the mic is quietly replaced with fresh tape.
success.art: A teenager scribbling furiously on a page of ad copy in a radio booth, a station manager reading over their shoulder delighted

failure.text: You run out of time mid-rewrite and read half of each version. The ad makes no sense, Sal threatens to sue and the manager pays you in mints. Somewhere in the transmitter, something laughs once.
failure.art: A station manager angrily on the phone in a radio office, a teenager slumped holding a crumpled page and a handful of mints

name: Rusty's Junkyard
blurb: Acres of rust behind a chain-link fence: a maze of stacked cars three high, a crusher that groans like a whale, Joey Benally's garage in a converted bus, and a basset hound who howls before trouble arrives.
art: A sprawling junkyard of rusted 1950s and 1970s cars stacked in towering rows behind a chain-link fence, a hulking car crusher, a converted school bus garage with tools hanging outside, a basset hound napping by the gate in hazy afternoon sun

beats.title: The Car Maze
beats.place: The stacks, Rusty's Junkyard
beats.text: Joey Benally needs a hubcap off a '57 Bel Air somewhere in the car maze, and he'll pay three quarters for it. The stacks are three cars high, the paths fork every twenty feet, and the junkyard maps never agree. Barnaby the basset hound plants himself at the entrance and refuses to go one step farther.
beats.art: A towering maze of rusted cars stacked three high in a junkyard, narrow dirt paths forking into shadow, a teenager at the entrance with a basset hound sitting stubbornly beside them

choices.label: Go in with a plan and a chalk mark at every turn

success.text: Chalk arrow, chalk arrow, Bel Air. You pop the hubcap, follow your arrows back out and hand it to Joey, who nods his highest compliment: "Not bad." Three quarters, and he lets you sit in the garage and drink his good soda.
success.art: A teenager holding up a gleaming chrome hubcap in a junkyard maze, chalk arrows marked on the rusted cars behind them

failure.text: Your chalk arrows are pointing the wrong way when you turn around. All of them. The path behind you is a wall of cars that wasn't there. You walk for an hour, and come out somewhere the maze shouldn't lead.
failure.art: A narrow junkyard path where every chalk arrow on the rusted cars points back the way a lost teenager came, a dead end of stacked cars ahead

choices.label: Coax Barnaby along and follow his nose

success.text: With half a hot dog and a lot of praise, Barnaby leads you on a crooked path that avoids every place he growls at. The Bel Air is right where he finally sits down. Moral of the story: always trust the dog.
success.art: A basset hound leading a teenager through a junkyard car maze, nose to the ground, a classic chrome car at the end of the path

failure.text: Barnaby leads you in, then stops, howls and bolts. You're alone in the stacks, and somewhere ahead, a car door creaks open and slams. You leave without the hubcap and Joey says, "Yeah, the dog knows."
failure.art: A basset hound running away down a junkyard path with ears flying, a teenager alone between towering stacks of rusted cars

beats.title: Something in the Trunk
beats.place: The crusher, Rusty's Junkyard
beats.text: Rusty is about to drop a 1959 Cadillac into the crusher, and from the trunk comes a knock. Three slow knocks. Rusty can't hear it over the engine and won't stop the job for "a teenager's imagination." The crusher plates are already grinding open like the jaws of something hungry.
beats.art: A hulking junkyard car crusher with its plates open, a crane lowering a pink 1959 Cadillac with tailfins toward it, a gruff man in the operator's seat, a teenager waving their arms frantically

choices.label: Climb onto the Cadillac and pop the trunk

success.text: You leap onto the tailfin and yank the trunk open. A family of raccoons pours out, along with a dusty steel box: a 1959 time capsule from the Glimmer Falls Elementary class, never buried. Rusty stops the crane and turns very red. He pays you not to tell anyone.
success.art: A teenager clinging to the tailfin of a pink Cadillac dangling from a crane, the trunk open, raccoons tumbling out with a dusty metal box

failure.text: You slip off the bumper and hit the dirt hard. The Cadillac drops into the crusher. The knocking stops before the plates close. You'll never know. That's the worst part.
failure.art: A teenager lying in junkyard dirt looking up at a crushed pink car between steel plates, dust hanging in the air

choices.label: Get Joey to make Rusty shut it down

success.text: Joey walks up, turns the key in the crusher's panel himself and says "Hear that?" Rusty finally hears the knocking. Inside the trunk: an old radio still tuned to KGLM, playing a station ID from 1959. Rusty gives it to you, spooked.
success.art: A young mechanic with a key in a crusher control panel, a gruff junkyard owner staring at an opened Cadillac trunk revealing a glowing vintage radio

failure.text: Rusty brushes you both off and drops the Cadillac. As the plates close, every car radio in the junkyard switches on at once to the same song, and then off. Rusty shuts down for the day without a word.
failure.art: Dozens of junked car dashboards lighting up at once across a dusk junkyard, a crushed Cadillac in the crusher

beats.title: Pay by the Pound
beats.place: The scrap scale, Rusty's Junkyard
beats.text: Rusty pays by the pound for copper and aluminum, and the old station wagons at the back are full of it. You have a wagon, a pair of pliers and the whole afternoon. The trouble is the back of the lot, where the wagons are parked in a circle facing inward, like they're having a meeting.
beats.art: A teenager pulling a rusty little red wagon heaped with copper wire and aluminum cans past a circle of old wood-paneled station wagons parked facing inward in a junkyard

choices.label: Strip wire fast and haul it to the scale

success.text: Two full wagonloads. Rusty weighs it, grumbles and pays you four quarters. In the last wagon you find a pair of walkie-talkies still in the box. Nobody's going to miss them.
success.art: A grimy, grinning teenager beside a junkyard scale stacked with copper wire, holding up a boxed pair of walkie-talkies

failure.text: You cut the wrong wire in the third wagon and every horn in the circle honks at once. You drop everything and run. When you go back for your wagon, it's parked in the middle of the circle, with them.
failure.art: A little red wagon sitting in the middle of a circle of old station wagons facing inward, headlights on in daylight

choices.label: Find the working radio and hum along while you work

success.text: One of the wagons has a radio that still works. You hum along, the circle of cars seems to settle, and the job goes easy. The radio's dial is stuck on a station that doesn't exist, playing a weather report for October 31, 1986. You write it down.
success.art: A teenager humming while stripping wire in the open door of a wood-paneled station wagon, its dashboard radio glowing, other cars around it

failure.text: You hum, and the radio hums back, a half-beat behind, in your voice. You haul one load and leave the rest. Rusty pays you a quarter and asks why you look like you saw a ghost.
failure.art: A junkyard car radio glowing alone on a dashboard in an empty car, a teenager walking briskly away with a half-empty wagon

beats.title: Wade's Van Won't Start
beats.place: Joey's garage bus, Rusty's Junkyard
beats.text: Wade Whitfield's van, a brown panel van with a wizard airbrushed on the side, won't start, and tonight is open-mic night at the Glitter Box. He's never read a poem out loud before. He's been trying to back out for a week, and now the van is giving him the excuse. He doesn't look relieved.
beats.art: A burnout metalhead with a mullet slumped against a brown van with a wizard airbrushed on the side, its hood up, a crumpled notebook of poems in his hand, a converted bus garage behind

choices.label: Get under the hood and fix it

success.text: It's the starter. You tap it with a wrench the way Joey taught you, and the van roars. Wade looks at the notebook, then at you. "Guess I gotta go now." His poem is about his little sister, and the Glitter Box gives him a standing ovation.
success.art: A teenager with a wrench under a van's hood as the engine roars to life, a metalhead in the driver's seat grinning nervously, a notebook on the dash

failure.text: You fix the starter and break the alternator. Joey sighs and promises to have it running by next week. Wade says "There's always next open mic," and you both know that's the excuse winning.
failure.art: A young mechanic sighing at a smoking van engine, a metalhead and a teenager standing beside it in the evening light

choices.label: Give him a ride on your handlebars

success.text: Two miles on handlebars with a six-foot metalhead is not a ride, it's a sport. You make it to the Glitter Box with three minutes to spare. Wade reads his poem with his voice cracking and his hands shaking, and Glory cries, and so does Wade.
success.art: A teenager pedaling a bicycle with a long-haired metalhead perched on the handlebars clutching a notebook, a sparkling theatre marquee ahead at dusk

failure.text: You hit a pothole on Elm and both go down. Wade's notebook goes into a storm drain. He sits on the curb a long time, then starts reciting the poem from memory to you, right there. It's good. He still doesn't go.
failure.art: A metalhead sitting on a curb beside a fallen bicycle reciting from memory to a teenager under a streetlight, a storm drain nearby

name: Oddment and Daughters
blurb: A traveling pawnshop that is never in the same lot twice: crammed shelves, a bell that rings before you touch the door, and Ms. Oddment behind the counter, who always has exactly what you need and always wants something odd in trade.
art: A narrow, crooked little shop wedged into an empty lot, its windows crammed with clocks, music boxes, dolls and brass curiosities, a hand-painted sign reading Oddment and Daughters, warm lamplight inside in broad daylight

beats.title: The Appraisal
beats.place: The counter, Oddment and Daughters
beats.text: Ms. Oddment is a tall woman in a velvet waistcoat with a jeweler's loupe on a chain and eyes the color of tea. She looks you up and down as if you were an estate sale. "I don't buy things, dear. I buy afternoons. Memories. A little bit of the way you laugh." She taps a brass scale. "What will you sell me?"
beats.art: A tall mysterious woman in a velvet waistcoat behind a cluttered antique pawnshop counter, a jeweler's loupe on a chain, a brass scale with empty pans, shelves of curios glowing in lamplight

choices.label: Sell her the memory of your worst birthday

success.text: She draws it out of you with a silver spoon, a little gray cloud, and drops it in a jar. You can't remember why you ever hated that cake. She pays you in quarters and throws in a deck of tarot cards. "They were already looking for you."
success.art: A tall woman lifting a small gray glowing cloud from a teenager's forehead with a silver spoon into a glass jar, a deck of tarot cards and coins on the counter

failure.text: She takes the wrong memory, the one of your best birthday. You can feel the gap where it was. She frowns, apologizes, and gives you three quarters you'd trade back in a heartbeat. "My hand slipped. It does, near Halloween."
failure.art: A glass jar on a pawnshop counter holding a warm golden glowing cloud, a woman looking apologetic, a teenager touching their temple

choices.label: Haggle her down to something harmless

success.text: You offer her your worst knock-knock joke. She laughs, a real laugh, and the lamps flare. "Done." She hands you a can of Aqua-Glow Max Hold. "Hairspray burns brighter than you'd think, and a bad joke is priceless."
success.art: A tall woman laughing behind a pawnshop counter, lamps flaring brightly, sliding a can of hairspray across to a grinning teenager

failure.text: Every offer you make, she counters with a stranger one: your shadow on Tuesdays, your middle name, the sound of your footsteps. You leave with nothing, and for an hour your footsteps make no sound at all.
failure.art: A teenager walking out of a crooked pawnshop onto a sunny sidewalk, oddly shadowless in the bright sun, a woman watching from the window

choices.label: Ask her what she does with it all

success.text: She looks at you a long moment. "Some things the world forgets, I keep. Some things the world should forget, I keep somewhere safer." She shows you a locked case at the back, very full and very quiet. "Everything cursed passes through a shop like mine eventually, dear. I only make sure it finds the right owner."
success.art: A tall woman holding a lamp beside a locked glass case at the back of a pawnshop, shadowy objects inside, a teenager peering in

failure.text: "Curiosity is a lovely currency," she says, and the brass scale tips as if you'd paid. You feel a little lighter and can't remember the name of your second-grade teacher. She smiles politely and rings up the sale.
failure.art: A brass pawnshop scale tipping under an invisible weight, a woman's long fingers ringing up a sale on an antique register

beats.title: All Sales Final
beats.place: The front door, Oddment and Daughters
beats.text: A sweating man in a golf visor is trying to return a snow globe of Glimmer Falls. "It shows tomorrow's weather," he babbles, "and tomorrow's weather has my house on fire in it." Ms. Oddment points at a sign: ALL SALES FINAL. He turns to you, holding it out, shaking. Inside the globe, tiny flames flicker over a tiny roof.
beats.art: A frantic man in a golf visor holding out a snow globe of a little town in a cramped pawnshop, tiny flames flickering inside the glass over one house, a tall shopkeeper pointing at a sign reading all sales final

choices.label: Take the globe off his hands for a quarter

success.text: The second it's yours, the flames inside go out and snow falls instead. The man nearly faints with relief. You set the globe on your windowsill. Every morning it shows the weather, honestly, and once, a warning you were glad to have.
success.art: A teenager holding a snow globe in which gentle snow falls over a tiny peaceful town, a relieved man in a golf visor sagging against a counter

failure.text: The moment you touch the glass, the tiny flames move from his roof to yours. Your roof. You put it down fast. Ms. Oddment takes it back for free with a sigh. "That's the trouble with gifts that see. They never lie, only change their minds."
failure.art: A snow globe on a pawnshop counter showing tiny flames over a different house, a teenager snatching their hand away

choices.label: Run to his house and check the wiring

success.text: His furnace has a cracked flue and a pile of dry newspapers stacked right against it. You move them, he calls a repairman and the flames in the globe shrink to a candle on a birthday cake. He tips you two quarters and a first-aid kit from his trunk.
success.art: A teenager pulling stacks of old newspapers away from a rusty basement furnace, a man in a golf visor on the phone, a snow globe on a shelf showing a small birthday candle

failure.text: You check everything and find nothing. That night, a fire truck rolls past your window with its siren off. In the morning, the man's house is fine, but his garage is a black square. The snow globe is back in Ms. Oddment's window.
failure.art: A suburban house with a burned-out garage beside it at dawn, a fire truck pulling away, smoke drifting

beats.title: One of the Daughters
beats.place: The back room, Oddment and Daughters
beats.text: Behind the beaded curtain a girl about your age is restocking a shelf of glass eyes. She has Ms. Oddment's tea-colored eyes and a name tag that says WEDNESDAY. "There are seven of us. We're never allowed out of the shop." She lowers her voice. "I want to see the mall. Just once. Will you take me?"
beats.art: A girl in an old-fashioned smock with tea-colored eyes restocking a shelf of glass eyes in a dim pawnshop back room, a beaded curtain behind her, a teenager peeking through

choices.label: Sneak her out the back for an hour

success.text: You take Wednesday to Starlight Mall. She eats a pretzel, rides the escalator six times and laughs at the fountain. When you bring her back, Ms. Oddment is waiting, arms crossed, then sighs and gives you a box of glow-stick bracelets. "For keeping her safe. Don't do it again. Do it again."
success.art: A girl with tea-colored eyes laughing on a mall escalator with a pretzel, a teenager beside her, neon lights all around

failure.text: The back door opens onto a different street, then a different town, then a field you don't recognize. Wednesday drags you back inside before the door forgets where it is. "It does that," she says, disappointed. "Next time."
failure.art: A pawnshop back door opening onto an unfamiliar misty field at noon, a girl yanking a teenager back inside by the sleeve

choices.label: Ask Ms. Oddment to let her go

success.text: Ms. Oddment listens, very still. Then she takes off her loupe. "My mother never let me out either." She hands Wednesday a coat. They walk out together, mother and daughter, for the first time in a very long time. The shop smells like rain.
success.art: A tall shopkeeper helping a girl into a coat at the door of a crooked pawnshop, both stepping out into afternoon sunlight

failure.text: "The world is not kind to things like us, dear," Ms. Oddment says gently, and closes the curtain. Wednesday waves through the beads. You hear a lock click, and you feel you just made something worse.
failure.art: A beaded curtain swaying closed in a dim pawnshop, a girl's hand waving through the beads, a tall shadow behind her

beats.title: The Things on the Shelves
beats.place: The aisles, Oddment and Daughters
beats.text: Ms. Oddment will pay a quarter a shelf to dust. "Don't touch anything that hums. Don't answer anything that asks you a question. And if the monkey with the cymbals starts clapping, leave the aisle at once." The first shelf has a music box, a baby shoe and a lighter engraved KEEP ME. The music box hums.
beats.art: A teenager with a feather duster in a narrow pawnshop aisle crammed with curios, a humming music box, a single baby shoe, an engraved lighter, a wind-up cymbal monkey on a high shelf watching

choices.label: Dust every shelf slowly and follow the rules

success.text: Four shelves, no touching, no answering. The music box asks you its question three times and you never answer. At the end, Ms. Oddment counts out four quarters and nods. "Most people answer." You don't ask what happens to them.
success.art: A teenager carefully dusting a pawnshop shelf around curios with careful fingertips, a shopkeeper counting coins into their palm at the end of the aisle

failure.text: The music box asks, "Do you want to know how it ends?" and you say "What?" before you can stop yourself. The cymbal monkey starts clapping. You run. Ms. Oddment pays you anyway, minus one quarter "for the excitement."
failure.art: A wind-up monkey clashing its cymbals on a high pawnshop shelf, a teenager sprinting down the aisle dropping a feather duster

choices.label: Slip the KEEP ME lighter into your pocket

success.text: You pocket it. It's warm. At the door, Ms. Oddment says without looking up, "Keep the flashlight too, then. You'll want light more than fire." When you check your pocket, the lighter is gone, and a heavy six-cell flashlight is in its place.
success.art: A teenager at a pawnshop door pulling a heavy flashlight out of their jacket pocket in surprise, a shopkeeper absorbed in her ledger

failure.text: The lighter burns your fingers, and you drop it. When you pick it up, the engraving reads KEEP ME AWAY. Ms. Oddment is standing right behind you. "Thieves dust for free, dear." You finish the shelves unpaid.
failure.art: An engraved silver lighter lying on a pawnshop floor, a teenager blowing on burnt fingertips, a tall shopkeeper standing right behind them

name: Mercy Valley Clinic
blurb: A flat-roofed 1960s walk-in clinic with a lollipop jar on every counter, a waiting-room TV stuck on one channel, and Nurse Inez Duarte, who has patched up every kid on Crystal Street and believes every word they tell her about the monsters.
art: A low flat-roofed 1960s walk-in clinic of pale green brick with a red cross painted above wide glass doors, potted marigolds and a wooden bench out front, a parked bicycle, a warm waiting room of orange plastic chairs glowing through big windows in bright afternoon sun

beats.title: Wipeout on Larkspur Hill
beats.place: The front walk, Mercy Valley Clinic
beats.text: A kid in a homemade daredevil cape comes off his BMX at the bottom of Larkspur Hill and skids right up to the clinic doors, howling. Nurse Inez is elbow-deep in a waiting room full of sniffles, so she points at you and then at the first-aid cart. "You. Wash your hands. Go." Behind the kid, his bike is still rolling. Uphill. Pedals turning all by themselves.
beats.art: A small boy in a homemade star-spangled cape sitting on a clinic front walk with a scraped knee, a teenager kneeling beside him with a white first-aid kit, a brisk nurse with silver-streaked curls waving through glass doors, a riderless BMX bike rolling uphill behind them, sunny autumn afternoon

choices.label: Clean the scrape and bandage it like a pro

success.text: You keep your voice low and calm, dab on the stinging stuff, count to three and fib that it's two. One butterfly bandage, one grape lollipop. Inez checks your work over the top of her glasses and nods. "Steady hands. Come back in a couple years and I'll put you on the schedule."
success.art: A teenager pressing a bandage onto a grinning boy's knee on a sunny clinic step, a brisk nurse with silver-streaked curls and a teal cardigan peering approvingly over her glasses, a purple lollipop clutched in the boy's fist, his cape spread on the concrete

failure.text: You get a good look at the scrape and your knees go to jelly. The kid ends up patting your back and telling you to breathe into a paper bag. Inez patches him up in forty seconds flat and hands the lollipop to you instead.
failure.art: A woozy teenager sitting on a clinic bench with their head between their knees breathing into a brown paper bag, a small caped boy patting their back, a nurse in a teal cardigan briskly bandaging the boy's knee in afternoon sun

choices.label: Distract him with a death-defying stunt special

success.text: You narrate his crash like a TV daredevil special: the jump, the wind, the cape, the crowd on its feet. By the slow-motion replay he's laughing too hard to notice the bandage going on. His mom tips you a quarter for the show, and he asks for your autograph on his knee.
success.art: A teenager gesturing like a TV announcer into a rolled-up magazine microphone, a caped boy laughing on a clinic step while a nurse in a teal cardigan wraps his knee, his mother in a windbreaker clapping, golden afternoon light

failure.text: Your dramatic reenactment ends with you tripping over the curb. Now there are two patients. Inez sighs the sigh of a woman who has seen this exact thing every Halloween since 1971 and hands you an ice pack shaped like a pumpkin.
failure.art: A teenager sprawled on a curb outside a green brick clinic holding a pumpkin-shaped ice pack to one elbow, a caped boy giggling on the step, a nurse with silver-streaked curls shaking her head with hands on her hips

choices.label: Chase the bike before it reaches the woods

success.text: You sprint up Larkspur Hill and grab the bike by the seat just as it noses into the pines. It shudders once, like a dog shaking off water, and goes still. There's a pinecone jammed in the spokes, and it's warm. You wheel it back down to a kid who now believes you can fly.
success.art: A teenager sprinting uphill and grabbing the seat of a riderless BMX bike at the edge of a pine forest, autumn leaves whirling around them, a small green brick clinic far below at the bottom of the hill, bright afternoon sky

failure.text: The bike beats you to the treeline and rolls into the shade under the pines. You stop at the edge, lungs burning. Somewhere in the dark between the trunks, something rings the bike bell twice, politely. The kid's mom says she'll just buy him a new one.
failure.art: A winded teenager bent over at the edge of a shadowy pine forest, a BMX bike vanishing between dark tree trunks, a chrome bike bell glinting deep in the gloom, late afternoon sun slanting across the hillside

beats.title: Candy Striper for a Day
beats.place: The short-stay ward, Mercy Valley Clinic
beats.text: Inez's volunteer called in sick, so you get the red-and-white striped smock and the gelatin cart. The three-bed short-stay ward holds a snoring mailman, a girl recovering from her tonsils with a stack of comic books, and Mrs. Esperanza Ochoa, 88, who says her late husband Teo visits every day at four. The ward clock says 3:58.
beats.art: A teenager in a red-and-white striped volunteer smock pushing a cart of wobbling lime gelatin cups into a small sunny clinic ward, an elderly woman in a crocheted shawl sitting up in bed watching the doorway, a round wall clock nearly at four

choices.label: Pull up a chair and ask Mrs. Ochoa about Teo

success.text: She tells you how Teo danced the mambo at the Grange Hall in 1949 and hummed while he fixed the sink. At four o'clock the curtain by her bed sways, and the room smells like aftershave and motor oil for exactly one minute. She squeezes your hand. "See? He likes you."
success.art: A teenager in a striped smock holding hands with a smiling elderly woman in a clinic bed, the curtain beside the bed swaying gently in golden afternoon light, a vase of carnations on the windowsill

failure.text: She tells you about Teo until four o'clock comes and goes with nothing at all. Her face falls. "He's never late." You stay with her until the dinner trays come, and you can't stop glancing at the empty chair by the window.
failure.art: An elderly woman in a clinic bed gazing at a vacant vinyl chair beside a sunny window, a teenager in a striped smock sitting quietly at her bedside, a dinner tray with a covered plate cooling on the side table

choices.label: Check the front desk's visitor sheets

success.text: Every day since September, at 4:00 on the dot, in shaky old-fashioned cursive: T. Ochoa, in and out. Inez reads it over your shoulder and doesn't blink. "He signs in, he signs out, he wipes his feet. Best-behaved visitor I've got." She pours you a cup of coffee like you're staff.
success.art: A teenager in a striped smock and a brisk nurse with silver-streaked curls leaning together over a clipboard at a clinic front desk, a long column of identical looping ink cursive, a mug of coffee steaming beside it

failure.text: You flip through the visitor sheets: T. Ochoa, every day at four, in the same shaky hand. Then you turn the last page and find tomorrow's date, already signed. The paper is cold as a freezer door. You put the clipboard down very carefully.
failure.art: A teenager in a striped smock holding a yellowed clipboard at arm's length over a clinic front desk, old visitor sheets fanned out across the counter, chilly blue light falling through the window blinds

choices.label: Wait in the hallway at four and see who comes

success.text: At four on the dot the hall lights hum and dim. Unhurried footsteps you can't see pass you, pause, and something pats your shoulder the way an old man thanks a kid who held the door. From the ward comes Mrs. Ochoa's laugh, bright as a girl's at a dance.
success.art: A teenager in a striped smock standing tall in a dim clinic hallway, overhead lights glowing low and amber, a trail of faint shining footprints on the polished linoleum leading toward a sunlit ward doorway

failure.text: The hall lights dim and you lose your nerve, ducking into the supply closet with the mops. Slow footsteps pass, and somebody hums a mambo. When you come out, there's a fresh red carnation on the gelatin cart, and you're pretty sure it's for you.
failure.art: A teenager in a striped smock peeking out of a cramped clinic supply closet full of mops into a dim amber hallway, a single red carnation resting on a cart of lime gelatin cups

beats.title: The Nose Jar
beats.place: The exam room cabinet, Mercy Valley Clinic
beats.text: Mercy Valley turns twenty-five this week, and Inez wants a lobby display of the Nose Jar: every object she has pulled out of a Glimmer Falls kid's nose, ear or sneaker since 1961. Marbles. A tiny silver board-game top hat. Forty-one popcorn kernels. Each has a paper tag in Inez's tidy hand. One small purple pebble has a tag with your name on it, dated November 1, 1986.
beats.art: A big glass apothecary jar tipped open on a clinic exam table, colorful marbles, a tiny silver board-game top hat, popcorn kernels and a small glowing purple pebble spilling out, little paper tags on strings, a teenager leaning in close under a hanging lamp

choices.label: Show Inez the tag and ask what it means

success.text: Inez turns the tag over and over. "That's my handwriting. I didn't write it." Then she does the most comforting thing any adult has done all week: she believes you completely, writes her home phone number on your hand, and says, "Whatever's coming, you come here first."
success.art: A brisk nurse with silver-streaked curls and a teal cardigan holding a small paper tag up to the window light, her other hand pressing a ballpoint pen to a teenager's open palm, a glass jar of marbles on the exam table

failure.text: Inez reads the tag, goes pale and tears it in half. "Somebody's idea of a joke." She says it too fast. For the rest of the afternoon she keeps finding reasons to walk past the exam room, checking that you're still there.
failure.art: A pale nurse in a teal cardigan tearing a small paper tag in half beside a glass jar of marbles, a worried teenager sitting on a crinkly exam table, afternoon sun striping through window blinds

choices.label: Catalog the whole jar for the anniversary display

success.text: You sort twenty-five years of nose treasures into a display a museum would envy, with a chart of the top objects by decade: marbles own the sixties, crayons the seventies. Inez is so delighted she hands you a tin of bandages and Bactine "for the week you're about to have."
success.art: A teenager arranging marbles, crayons, buttons and tiny toys in neat rows on a felt-lined tray at a clinic counter, a smiling nurse with silver-streaked curls holding out a white tin first-aid kit

failure.text: You sort for an hour. Every time you look away, the purple pebble is back on top of the pile, no matter where you put it. Inez finds you staring at it, and without a word she locks the whole jar in the cabinet.
failure.art: A small purple pebble perched on top of a heap of marbles and buttons on a clinic counter, a teenager staring at it with narrowed eyes, a nurse in a teal cardigan reaching for a ring of cabinet keys

choices.label: Slip the humming pebble into your pocket

success.text: It hums against your leg all afternoon like a purring cat. It goes quiet by the lollipop jar and buzzes by any window that faces Crystal Street. Somebody filed this pebble under your name, and you intend to find out why. Until then, it's a pretty good weirdness detector.
success.art: A teenager walking down a clinic hallway with a faint violet glow shining through their jeans pocket, a glass lollipop jar on the counter beside them, a sunny window looking out on a suburban cul-de-sac

failure.text: Inez clocks it the second the pebble leaves the jar. "Pocket," she says, palm out, the way she's said it to every Crystal Street kid since Kennedy. You hand it over. It's warm, and her eyebrows climb all the way up.
failure.art: A brisk nurse with silver-streaked curls holding out an open palm toward a sheepish teenager, a small glowing purple pebble resting in the teenager's hand between them, a glass jar of marbles on the exam table

beats.title: The Halloween Binder
beats.place: The night desk, Mercy Valley Clinic
beats.text: Inez's night desk hides a fat orange binder marked HALLOWEEN WEEK, one page per kid, every year since 1961. Glitter burns that won't wash off. A lunchbox chewed by something with far too many tiny teeth. A boy who walked in with his shadow on backwards. She catches you looking. "Nobody else believes them," she says. "So I write it all down."
beats.art: A fat orange three-ring binder open on a cluttered clinic night desk under a gooseneck lamp, taped instant photos of grinning kids with bandaged elbows, a mug of coffee, a nurse with silver-streaked curls and a teal cardigan leaning on the counter beside a curious teenager

choices.label: Tell her what you've seen this week

success.text: You tell her everything, even the parts that sound ridiculous out loud. Inez doesn't laugh once. She takes a fresh page, writes your name across the top and underlines it twice. "Now it's on the record," she says. "And now somebody's watching your back."
success.art: A teenager talking earnestly across a clinic night desk, a nurse with silver-streaked curls listening intently with a pen poised over an open orange binder, warm gooseneck lamplight pooling between them

failure.text: You start to tell her, and the words jam up somewhere behind your teeth. Inez waits, then slides a cherry lollipop across the desk. "When you're ready. I'm here till midnight and back at seven." You leave with the lollipop and the story still stuck.
failure.art: A teenager slumped at a clinic night desk turning a red lollipop in their fingers, a patient nurse in a teal cardigan waiting with folded hands under a gooseneck lamp, an orange binder closed between them

choices.label: Read the binder cover to cover

success.text: Twenty-five Halloweens of patterns. The worst nights cluster on the same few streets, and the kids who came in together always healed faster than the ones who came in alone. You copy the useful parts into your notebook. Inez's binder is the best monster manual in California.
success.art: A teenager curled in an orange plastic waiting-room chair poring over a fat orange binder, a spiral notebook balanced on one knee, taped instant photos of smiling bandaged kids on the open pages, afternoon light through the windows

failure.text: Somewhere around 1979 the pages start describing kids you know, with dates that haven't happened yet. You shut the binder fast. Inez takes it back and doesn't ask what you saw, which is somehow worse.
failure.art: A wide-eyed teenager snapping a fat orange binder shut at a clinic night desk, a nurse with silver-streaked curls reaching to take it back, the gooseneck lamp flickering over a cold cup of coffee

name: Thriftee-Mart
blurb: The only supermarket in Glimmer Falls: buzzing fluorescent aisles, a Halloween candy aisle stacked to the ceiling, a manager who flinches at every price, and a bag boy who hears every rumor in town before it happens.
art: A sprawling 1980s supermarket storefront with wide plate-glass windows, a pyramid of orange pumpkins and a row of shopping carts out front, bright fluorescent aisles glowing inside, a bag boy in a red apron pushing a long train of carts across a sunny parking lot

beats.title: Sticker Shock
beats.place: Aisle 2, canned goods, Thriftee-Mart
beats.text: Mr. Pettibone, the manager, is sweating through his short-sleeved dress shirt. His pricing gun has gone haywire: every sticker it spits out says 13 cents, the price of a can of ham at the 1959 grand opening, and half the aisle is already tagged. Shoppers are filling carts like it's the end of the world. "It's possessed," he whispers. "Or it's under warranty."
beats.art: A sweating supermarket manager in a short-sleeved shirt and clip-on tie clutching a hand-held pricing gun that spits a long curling ribbon of orange stickers, cheerful shoppers piling canned hams into carts under buzzing fluorescent lights

choices.label: Grab a sticker roll and re-price the aisle by hand

success.text: You go shelf by shelf at a speed that makes the stock boys whistle, peeling off 13-cent stickers and slapping on real ones. By noon the aisle is sane again. Mr. Pettibone presses two quarters into your hand like he's donating a kidney.
success.art: A teenager racing along a supermarket shelf of canned goods peeling off orange price stickers, a manager in a clip-on tie watching in grateful awe, two stock boys whistling from a rolling ladder under fluorescent light

failure.text: You re-price the entire aisle. When you step back to admire it, every new sticker has quietly changed to 13 cents too. Mr. Pettibone has to sit down on a case of creamed corn and breathe into his tie.
failure.art: A supermarket manager slumped on a cardboard case of creamed corn holding his clip-on tie to his face, a teenager staring at a long shelf of cans dotted with identical orange stickers

choices.label: Talk Mr. Pettibone down off the ledge

success.text: You walk him to the break room, get him a paper cup of water, and point out that a town that buys cheap ham today will buy full-price mustard all week. He laughs for the first time since 1983 and makes you an honorary assistant manager, plastic name tag and all.
success.art: A teenager handing a paper cup of water to a frazzled supermarket manager in a tiny break room with a dented coffee maker and a cluttered corkboard, the manager smiling weakly, a plastic name tag in his other hand

failure.text: Halfway through your pep talk, the pricing gun fires on its own and tags the intercom, which squeals like a stuck pig. Mr. Pettibone locks himself in the walk-in freezer to "think," and you get stuck covering the courtesy desk, getting yelled at about coupons.
failure.art: A teenager stuck behind a supermarket courtesy desk facing a line of annoyed shoppers waving clipped coupons, a heavy walk-in freezer door shut tight in the background, frost curling from its seams

choices.label: Pull the trigger yourself and see what it wants

success.text: You squeeze the trigger and the gun prints one sticker that says THANK YOU in a curly old store font, then a normal price, then another. Folded tight behind the roll you find a yellowed 1959 grand-opening coupon. Old store, old ghosts, small favors. The gun behaves after that.
success.art: A teenager holding a hand-held pricing gun up to the fluorescent light, a tiny yellowed coupon unfolding from inside its roll, a curl of orange stickers drifting down around them like confetti

failure.text: The gun bucks in your hand and fires a sticker square onto your forehead: 13 cents. It will not come off. Kids in the parking lot point and laugh, and for the rest of the day every stray cat in Glimmer Falls follows you at a respectful distance.
failure.art: A teenager with a bright orange price sticker stuck to the middle of their forehead walking across a sunny supermarket parking lot, a parade of curious stray cats trailing behind them, kids pointing from a station wagon

beats.title: Paper, Plastic or Rumor
beats.place: Checkout lane 4, Thriftee-Mart
beats.text: Dez Farrow has bagged groceries for half of Glimmer Falls, and he hears everything: who's getting divorced, who bought forty cans of hairspray, who keeps buying cat food with no cat. He trades rumors for favors, never money. Today he leans over the bagging counter and whispers that one shopping cart in the lot rolls off toward the old quarry end every night, by itself.
beats.art: A lanky teen bag boy in a red apron and paper hat leaning conspiratorially over a checkout lane toward a listening teenager, brown paper grocery bags and a conveyor belt of cereal boxes, a lone shopping cart drifting across the parking lot beyond the window

choices.label: Help him round up the carts in the lot

success.text: You and Dez snake a train of thirty carts across the blacktop and slam it home. He pays up with a whole afternoon of gossip, including which houses on Crystal Street keep their porch lights on all night, and why. Hold a rumor right and it's a map.
success.art: A teenager and a bag boy in a red apron pushing a long snaking train of shopping carts across a sunny supermarket parking lot, autumn leaves skittering under the wheels, the store windows glowing behind them

failure.text: The cart train jackknifes and rolls into the side of Mr. Pettibone's station wagon. Dez winces. "Rumors are on hold until I'm not fired." One cart breaks loose and rolls away toward the quarry end of the lot, in no hurry at all.
failure.art: A tangle of shopping carts crashed against the side of a wood-paneled station wagon, a bag boy in a red apron covering his face with both hands, a single cart rolling away across the far end of the parking lot

choices.label: Trade him a juicy rumor of your own

success.text: You tell him the one about the vice principal and the karaoke contest, with voices and a dance break. Dez is so delighted he pays you back three rumors and a free Bolt Cola from the checkout cooler. "You," he says, "are wasted on honesty."
success.art: A teenager acting out a dramatic story with jazz hands at a supermarket checkout lane, a bag boy in a paper hat doubled over laughing and holding out a cold bottle of cola from a glowing cooler

failure.text: Your rumor bombs. Worse, Dez already heard it, and a better version. By closing time there's a brand-new rumor going around the Thriftee-Mart about you, and somehow it involves a llama.
failure.art: A deflated teenager at a checkout lane while a bag boy in a paper hat whispers behind his hand to a giggling cashier with a teased perm, paper grocery bags stacked high between them

choices.label: Watch the wandering cart at closing time

success.text: At closing, the cart rolls out of its corral and heads for the quarry end of the lot, and you walk right beside it. It stops at a storm drain, wheels pointed down, waiting. You wheel it back and tie it to the corral with your shoelace. In the morning it's still there, and Dez looks at you like you hung the moon.
success.art: A teenager walking calmly beside a lone shopping cart rolling across a dusky supermarket parking lot toward a storm drain, long shadows stretching under tall sodium lights, a violet sunset over the foothills

failure.text: The cart turns to face you. That's all it does. It just faces you, for a long time, one wheel squeaking softly, while the parking-lot lights buzz on one by one. You walk home the long way, and you don't look back until your own porch.
failure.art: A shopping cart sitting alone in a vast dusky parking lot turned toward a frozen teenager, a row of tall parking lot lights flickering on one after another into the distance

beats.title: The Last Bag of Full-Size Bars
beats.place: Aisle 7, Halloween candy, Thriftee-Mart
beats.text: The candy aisle is a fortress of orange and black: Three Muskrateers, Reesey's Pieces, Kit-Kaboom and, at the very end, one last bag of full-size Choco-Lotta bars. Two Crystal Street moms have their hands on it and neither one is letting go. Meanwhile, from somewhere deep inside the giant candy-corn pyramid, comes a steady, happy crunching.
beats.art: A towering supermarket Halloween candy display of orange and black bags stacked to the ceiling beside a giant pyramid of candy corn, two determined moms in pastel sweatsuits tugging a bag of chocolate bars between them, a teenager stepping in with hands raised

choices.label: Broker a peace treaty between the moms

success.text: You propose joint custody: they split the bag and team up on one haunted garage for both houses, double the scares. They shake on it like heads of state. Each one slips you a quarter, and one of them asks if you're available to babysit.
success.art: A teenager holding up a bag of chocolate bars between two moms in pastel sweatsuits shaking hands in an orange and black candy aisle, each mom pressing a coin into the teenager's free palm

failure.text: Both moms turn on you at once. They storm off in opposite directions, and you're left holding the bag, which Mr. Pettibone makes you pay for because "it's been squeezed."
failure.art: A teenager left holding a crumpled bag of chocolate bars in an orange and black candy aisle, two moms storming away in opposite directions, a manager in a clip-on tie approaching with his hand out

choices.label: Dig into the candy-corn pyramid to find the cruncher

success.text: You plunge both arms into the pyramid and haul out a raccoon in a tiny striped sweater, fat as a pillow and deeply unbothered. The whole aisle laughs. The sweater is stitched BANDIT. You carry him out to the parking lot, where a very relieved old man has been calling his name for an hour.
success.art: A teenager hauling a plump raccoon in a little striped sweater out of a collapsing pyramid of candy corn, kernels cascading everywhere, laughing shoppers crowding the bright supermarket aisle

failure.text: The pyramid collapses on you in an avalanche of candy corn. When you dig yourself out, the crunching has stopped, and every kernel within a yard of you has one neat little bite taken out of it. Whatever it was, it has very small teeth, and it got away.
failure.art: A teenager buried to the shoulders in a heap of spilled candy corn in a supermarket aisle, nibbled kernels scattered all around, a small furry striped tail disappearing under the bottom shelf

choices.label: Build a display so spectacular nobody wants to fight

success.text: You build a candy castle with turrets of Kit-Kaboom, a drawbridge of Choco-Lotta bars and a moat of Bolt Cola cans. Shoppers stop to take pictures. Mr. Pettibone doesn't know what to do with his face, so he hands you a six-cell flashlight off the endcap. "For the week," he mutters.
success.art: A teenager placing the final candy bar on a towering castle built of Halloween candy bags with a moat of soda cans, a supermarket manager staring open-mouthed, shoppers snapping instant photos in bright fluorescent light

failure.text: Your castle looks magnificent for nine whole seconds. Then a toddler pulls one bar out of the bottom row. They hear the collapse in the parking lot. Mr. Pettibone just points at the mop.
failure.art: A collapsed heap of Halloween candy bags and rolling soda cans spread across a supermarket floor, a triumphant toddler holding up a single candy bar, a teenager gripping a mop and bucket

beats.title: Price Check, Aisle Zero
beats.place: The courtesy desk, Thriftee-Mart
beats.text: Thriftee-Mart has twelve aisles. The intercom keeps calling for a price check on aisle zero. It's Mr. Pettibone's voice, and Mr. Pettibone is standing right next to you holding a cantaloupe, looking ill. "I haven't touched that microphone," he says. "I'm a produce man." At the back of the store, past frozen foods, a pair of swinging doors you've never noticed is gently swaying.
beats.art: A pale supermarket manager in a clip-on tie holding a cantaloupe and staring up at a ceiling speaker, a teenager beside him, a pair of dented swinging doors gently swaying at the far end of a long fluorescent frozen-food aisle

choices.label: Push through the swinging doors and find aisle zero

success.text: Behind the doors is a 1959 grocery aisle, perfectly stocked and mint: tins of things they don't make anymore, a crank cash register, glass bottles of soda with the old formula. A radio plays a doo-wop song you almost know. You tip your head to the aisle like a guest, back out, and the doors settle shut, calm and satisfied.
success.art: A teenager with a flashlight standing in a perfectly stocked 1959 grocery aisle of tin cans and glass soda bottles, a brass crank cash register and a wooden tabletop radio, dust glittering in a single warm beam of light

failure.text: Behind the doors is a stockroom that goes back much farther than the building does. The fluorescent tubes buzz on ahead of you one at a time, inviting. You back out and let the doors swing shut. The intercom says, very softly, "Price check cancelled."
failure.art: A teenager backing out through swinging doors from an impossibly long stockroom of stacked cardboard boxes, fluorescent tubes flickering on one by one into the far distance

choices.label: Grab the courtesy-desk microphone and answer it

success.text: "Attention, Thriftee-Mart shoppers," you purr in your best late-night DJ voice, "aisle zero is closed for the season. Please enjoy ten percent off courage." The whole store applauds. The intercom crackles once, like a laugh, and goes back to soft-rock elevator music.
success.art: A teenager leaning into a gooseneck microphone at a supermarket courtesy desk with a sultry late-night DJ grin, shoppers in the aisles turning to applaud, a manager hiding a laugh behind a cantaloupe

failure.text: You key the mic, and your own voice comes out of the ceiling speakers a full second before you speak, saying something slightly different. The whole store hears it. Mr. Pettibone gently takes the microphone and puts it in a drawer.
failure.art: A startled teenager pulling back from a gooseneck microphone at a supermarket courtesy desk, a manager reaching to take it, shoppers frozen mid-aisle staring up at the ceiling speakers

choices.label: Dig the store blueprints out of the manager's office

success.text: The 1959 plans show thirteen aisles. Aisle zero was walled off after the grand opening because "customers reported feeling watched by the canned peaches." You and Mr. Pettibone agree to leave it be and stack pumpkins in front of the wall. He's so relieved he tips you two quarters.
success.art: A teenager and a supermarket manager unrolling yellowed architectural blueprints across a cluttered office desk, a coffee mug pinning one corner and a cantaloupe holding down another, a desk lamp glowing

failure.text: You find the blueprints, but someone has been at them first: aisle zero is circled over and over in red grease pencil. Mr. Pettibone swears he's never seen those circles. You both agree, out loud, to stop looking at blueprints for the day.
failure.art: Yellowed store blueprints spread across a desk with one narrow aisle circled again and again in red grease pencil, a teenager and a supermarket manager staring down at it under a buzzing desk lamp
